lessons: Open an exposition by naming its reader, why the result matters to them, what they will be able to do at the end, and a roadmap that previews the payoffs; open each section with where it is going and close it with what was gained.

For every linked formal result, say whether the formal statement is the same as, stronger than, or weaker than the prose claim and how; check the recorded statement reviews and say when none covers the linked declaration or when it is stale.

When an analysis uses an ideal process built from unknown quantities, say before introducing it that the algorithm never computes them, and specify the process on every history, including absorbing and failure states.
State a per-step failure bound together with the histories on which it holds; outside them, say what happens and why it is harmless.
When a lower bound controls "reaching" a hidden object, name guessing explicitly and bound the joint event, never success conditional on a cheap run.
A counterexample that redefines a random choice must define it on every branch, including the empty one, before claiming a marginal law.
Keep every lemma statement that later steps use outside optional boxes; box only proofs.
Collect every cost term into one total before simplifying to an explicit exponent, and move loose numeric constants to the long record.
Turn every prose pointer to the long record into an anchor link at the passage, keeping the section number for print.
Inspect float behaviour at the page budget: a figure taller than the float-page fraction produces a page with no text.
